title: Book 5 — Terpsichore, Chapter 63
paragraphs: Then, as the Athenians say, these men, settled at Delphi, persuaded the Pythian priestess by gifts of money that whenever men of the Spartans should come to consult the oracle, whether privately or publicly, she should propose to them to set Athens free. The Lacedaemonians, since the same utterance was delivered to them on all occasions, sent Anchimolius son of Aster, a man of repute among their citizens, with an army to drive the sons of Peisistratus out of Athens—even though these were very closely connected with them by guest-friendship; for they held that the concerns of the god should be preferred to those of men. This force they sent by sea in ships. Anchimolius, having put in to shore at Phalerum, disembarked his army; but the sons of Peisistratus, having learned of this beforehand, called in an auxiliary force from Thessaly, for they had made an alliance with the Thessalians, and the Thessalians at their request sent by public resolution a body of a thousand horse and also their king Cineas, a man of Conium. With these as allies, the sons of Peisistratus devised the following: they cut down the trees in the plain of Phalerum and made this district fit for horsemen to ride over, and then they sent the cavalry to attack the enemy's camp; and falling upon it, they killed (among many other Lacedaemonians) Anchimolius himself, and the survivors they shut up in their ships. Such was the outcome of the first expedition from Lacedaemon; and the burial-place of Anchimolius is at Alopece in Attica, near the temple of Heracles at Cynosarges.
